Appreciate the clear list. We can provide a purpose-built runbook and the requested artifacts. High-level answers first, then I attached a draft runbook and an architecture diagram for quick review. Full test artifacts will follow tomorrow.

Summary (Dedicated GPU pools):
- Physical isolation: Dedicated customers are allocated exclusive GPU devices within a reserved pool. We do not colocate multiple Dedicated customer workloads on the same GPU device.
- Scheduling and allocation: The orchestration layer assigns devices using tenant affinity tags and a placement engine that enforces "device-exclusive" leases. Leases are recorded in the allocation log (UUIDs) and are visible in audit events.
- Runtime separation: Each allocation runs in a tenant-scoped runtime (container + process namespace). The inference runtime enforces per-tenant KV namespaces; the in-memory KV cache uses a tenant ID prefix + namespace partitioning (no shared global cache buckets for Dedicated pools).
- Eviction & failover runbook (high level): autonomous eviction is triggered when hardware is marked unhealthy, on scheduled maintenance, or when operator-initiated rebalancing is required. Eviction workflow preserves model state (checkpoint to ephemeral store) and routes traffic to a fallback model variant in under the configured 5-minute SLO for reserved capacity.

Attachments included: redwood_dedicated-tenant-separation-runbook-v1.pdf (draft), isolation-architecture-diagram.pdf. I'll run the noisy-neighbor stress bench and upload results by EOD Monday.

Lena — quick technical follow-up from the runtime team with specifics you asked about: 

1) KV cache isolation: we use per-tenant namespaces in the runtime cache. Keys are namespaced and stored in tenant-specific partitions; eviction and LRU policies are per-partition. There is no cross-tenant pointer/reference or shared allocation for Dedicated pools.

2) Memory & device isolation: For Dedicated devices we bind the GPU device node to the tenant container; the kernel device file is not accessible to other tenants. We use cgroup v2 to set device-access controls and enforce memory limits at the process level. 

3) Noisy-neighbor mitigation controls: 
   - Scheduling: avoid packing by design for Dedicated pools (we place one tenant per GPU unless explicit co-reservation requested).
   - Runtime throttles: we apply per-tenant CUDA stream concurrency limits and per-tenant compute QoS knobs when needed.
   - Eviction policy: automated health-check probes -> drain connections -> checkpoint model state -> notify operator -> reassign device. Operators can also perform manual eviction; both flows emit an audit event.

4) Audit logging: allocation, revoke, health-check, and eviction events are emitted to the control-plane audit log (JSON lines with lease_uuid, tenant_id, node_id, timestamp). Retention is 90 days by default for Dedicated customers; longer retention is available as an add-on.

I've attached a small CSV with our first noisy-neighbor bench run (noisy-neighbor-test-results-20260713.csv). Results show p99 token latency impact <= 12% with our default throttles and zero cross-tenant cache contamination. We'll include the raw logs and a sanitized allocation audit snippet in the next upload.
